passages.t: The wedding banquet: the invited guests refuse
passages.happening:
Jesus speaks to the leaders in parables again. The kingdom of heaven is like a king who prepares a wedding banquet for his son. He sends his servants to call the invited guests, but they refuse to come. He sends other servants: ‘Tell those who have been invited that I have prepared my dinner. My oxen and fattened cattle have been killed, and everything is ready. Come to the wedding banquet.’

But the guests pay no attention. One goes off to his field, another to his business. The rest seize the servants, mistreat them and kill them. “The king was enraged, and he sent his troops to destroy those murderers and burn their city” (verse 7).

Then he tells his servants that the banquet is ready, but those invited were not worthy. ‘Go therefore to the crossroads and invite to the banquet as many as you can find.’ The servants go out into the streets and gather everyone they can find, “both evil and good,” and the wedding hall is filled with guests (verse 10).
passages.hearers:
This is the third of the stories Jesus tells the leaders in the temple courts, after the two sons and the tenants. Luke has a similar story of a great dinner (Luke 14:15-24), but in Matthew the host is a king, the feast is for his son's wedding, and the story is much darker.

A wedding feast for a king's son was the greatest feast anyone could be invited to. In the story the guests had already been invited. The servants come to tell them the food is ready. To refuse then, and go off to a field or a shop, was to say that ordinary business mattered more than the king. To kill his messengers was rebellion.

Hearers would catch who the servants stood for. God's messengers, the prophets, had been sent again and again and mistreated, as in the parable of the tenants just before (21:34-36). And Jesus had already pictured the kingdom as a feast: “many will come from the east and the west to share the banquet with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob” (8:11).

The new guests are gathered from the crossroads, ‘both evil and good’. Nobody earned a place. The hall is full of people who were never on the first list, like the tax collectors and prostitutes going into the kingdom ahead of the leaders (21:31).
passages.ot:
The prophets pictured the age to come as a feast. Isaiah promised, “On this mountain the LORD of Hosts will prepare a banquet for all the peoples, a feast of aged wine, of choice meat, of finely aged wine” (Isaiah 25:6). The prophets also pictured God's love for his people as a marriage: “I will betroth you to Me forever” (Hosea 2:19).

Zephaniah spoke of the day of the LORD as a sacrifice to which God invites guests: “the LORD has prepared a sacrifice; He has consecrated His guests” (Zephaniah 1:7).
passages.hard:
Does verse 7 describe the Romans burning Jerusalem in AD 70? A king sending troops to burn a city is a strange detail in a story about a wedding feast. Many scholars think Matthew, writing after the war, was pointing to the fall of Jerusalem, when the city and its temple burned, and they count this verse among the reasons for dating Matthew after 70. Others answer that destroying and burning a rebel city was common language in the Old Testament and in the ancient world for how a king punished rebels, so the verse needs no hindsight. Some point to Isaiah, where God's anger burns like fire against those who “have rejected the instruction of the LORD of Hosts” (Isaiah 5:24). These notes do not choose.

Whichever is right, the verse speaks of a judgment on people who refused the king and killed his messengers. It is not a verdict on the Jewish people. Jesus, the first guests at his own table, and all the servants who carried the invitation in Matthew's story were Jews.
passages.asks: The first guests did not hate the king. They were busy, one with his field, one with his business. Ask what ordinary thing in your life most often answers God's invitation with ‘not now’. And notice who filled the hall in the end: people from the roads, good and bad, who simply came when they were asked.

passages.t: The guest without wedding clothes, and ‘many are called’
passages.happening:
When the king comes in to see the guests, he sees a man who is not dressed in wedding clothes. ‘Friend,’ the king asks, ‘how did you get in here without wedding clothes?’ The man is speechless. Then the king tells the servants to tie him hand and foot and throw him into the outer darkness, “where there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth” (verse 13).

Jesus ends the story with a saying: “For many are called, but few are chosen” (verse 14).

This part of the story is found only in Matthew.
passages.hearers:
Many readers take ‘wedding clothes’ to mean clean clothes, a guest's best, as against the dirty clothes of work and the road. To come to a king's feast without them was to treat it as nothing special.

‘Friend’ is a polite word with an edge. Matthew uses it only three times, each time to someone in the wrong: to the grumbling worker (20:13), here, and to Judas in the garden (26:50). The king gives the man a chance to answer. He has nothing to say.

A later Jewish parable makes a good comparison. The Babylonian Talmud, put together several centuries after Jesus, tells in the name of Rabban Yohanan ben Zakkai of a king who invited his servants to a banquet without saying when. The wise ones dressed and waited at the palace door. The foolish went back to their work. When the call came suddenly, the wise came in dressed and the foolish came in dirty, and only the dressed ones sat down to eat (Shabbat 153a). There, as here, the clothes stand for being ready.

‘The outer darkness’ and ‘weeping and gnashing of teeth’ are Matthew's usual words for being shut out of the kingdom (8:12; 25:30).
passages.ot:
Isaiah used clothing as a picture of what God gives: “He has clothed me with garments of salvation and wrapped me in a robe of righteousness, as a bridegroom wears a priestly headdress” (Isaiah 61:10). The Teacher in Ecclesiastes said, “Let your garments always be white” (Ecclesiastes 9:8).

The New Testament picks up the picture. Paul told believers, “all of you who were baptized into Christ have clothed yourselves with Christ” (Galatians 3:27), and in Revelation the bride at the Lamb's wedding “was given clothing of fine linen, bright and pure,” which is “the righteous acts of the saints” (Revelation 19:8).
passages.hard:
Why throw out a man who was pulled in off the street? It can look unfair. The servants gathered everyone, ‘both evil and good’, with no warning, and then the king punishes one man for what he is wearing.

Some have suggested that the host gave wedding clothes to every guest at the door, so the man had refused a gift. It is an attractive idea, but there is no clear evidence of such a custom, and it should be held loosely. More weight falls on the story itself. The man is asked, and he has no excuse. The others were dressed. He could have been.

What do the clothes stand for? Christians have answered in several ways. Many Protestants read them as the righteousness God gives, a gift put on by faith (Isaiah 61:10). Many others, Catholic and Orthodox among them, read them as a life changed by grace, love and good works, and note how often Matthew stresses doing the Father's will (7:21). Many readers hold both together: the invitation is free to all, and grace does not leave a guest unchanged.

‘Many are called, but few are chosen’ is read in more than one way too. Some read ‘chosen’ as those God has chosen, whose choosing shows in how they answer. Others read it as those who accept the call and are found ready. A Jewish writing from the end of the first century, known as 4 Ezra, has a similar saying about the many who were made and the few who will be saved (4 Ezra 8:3). Jesus' saying sums up the whole story: many were invited, and not all who heard the call came, or came ready.

This saying is not meant to make an anxious person despair. In the story the doors were opened to everyone on the roads. The man thrown out was not someone afraid he was not good enough. He was someone who came in and did not care to be changed. If you are worried whether God will have you, notice that the king's invitation went out to ‘as many as you can find’.
passages.asks: The man wanted the feast without honouring the king. Ask whether you want the gifts of God without being changed by him. And if you fear you are not dressed well enough for God's table, hear what the prophets and apostles say: the clothes are his gift before they are your effort.

passages.t: What belongs to Caesar, and what belongs to God
passages.happening:
Then the Pharisees go out and plan to trap Jesus in his words. They send their disciples to him along with the Herodians. They begin with flattery: “we know that You are honest and that You teach the way of God in accordance with the truth” (verse 16). Then the question: “Is it lawful to pay taxes to Caesar or not?”

Jesus knows their evil intent. “You hypocrites, why are you testing Me? Show Me the coin used for the tax” (verses 18-19). They bring him a denarius, a silver coin. “Whose image is this,” he asks, “and whose inscription?” “Caesar’s,” they answer. Jesus tells them, “Give to Caesar what is Caesar’s, and to God what is God’s.” They are amazed, and they leave him and go away.
passages.hearers:
Mark tells this scene too (Mark 12:13-17), and the note on Mark 12 explains it. The Pharisees were teachers of the law, popular with ordinary people. The Herodians were supporters of the Herod family, who ruled with Rome's backing. These two groups did not usually work together.

The tax was a sore point. In AD 6 Rome took direct control of Judea and held a census so that it could tax the people. A man called Judas the Galilean led a revolt against it, teaching that God alone was Israel's master (Acts 5:37). So if Jesus said ‘Pay’, many in the crowd would think he had sided with Rome. If he said ‘Don't pay’, he could be reported to the Roman governor as a rebel.

The usual silver denarius of the emperor Tiberius showed his head, crowned with a wreath. Its Latin words called him ‘Tiberius Caesar Augustus, son of the divine Augustus’. We cannot be sure which coin they handed Jesus, but a coin like this carried both a human image and a claim to be divine. Notice that Jesus does not have one. His questioners do.

Matthew adds two things. Jesus calls the questioners ‘hypocrites’, people acting a part, since their praise was a mask for a trap. And he asks for ‘the coin used for the tax’, the very coin the argument was about.
passages.ot: Many readers hear in Jesus' word ‘image’ the first chapter of the Bible: “So God created man in His own image” (Genesis 1:27). They hear the point. The coin bears Caesar's image, so give it to him. You bear God's image, so give yourself to God.
passages.hard:
What does Jesus mean, and how does it apply to Christians and governments? Readers have taken it in more than one way, and Christians in different traditions weigh these differently.

One reading sees two real spheres. Government has a true but limited claim, such as taxes, and God has the greater claim. The word ‘give’ here can mean ‘give back’, as when paying a debt. Paul later writes, “Pay everyone what you owe him: taxes to whom taxes are due” (Romans 13:7). Another reading stresses that the second half swallows the first. Everything belongs to God, Caesar included, so Caesar's claim is small and his claim to be divine is false. When rulers later forbade the apostles to preach, they answered, “We must obey God rather than men” (Acts 5:29). A third reading notes that Jesus' answer is clever on purpose. He avoids the trap and leaves his hearers to work out what truly belongs to Caesar.

What all agree on is this. Jesus refused to let either side make him a tool of their cause. And no ruler, of any party, gets what belongs only to God. This exchange is not a ruling on any party, tax law or government of today, and it should not be pressed into service for one.
passages.asks: The question was meant to force Jesus onto a side. He would not be used. Ask whether you have let a political side take a place in your heart that belongs to God. Then ask the deeper question. You carry God's image. What would it mean to give him all of yourself?

passages.t: Whose wife will she be? The God of the living
passages.happening:
That same day some Sadducees come to Jesus. They say there is no resurrection. They remind him of a law of Moses: if a man dies with no children, his brother is to marry the widow and raise children for him. Now there were seven brothers. The first married and died childless, and so did the second and the third, down to the seventh. Last of all the woman died. “In the resurrection, then, whose wife will she be of the seven?” (verse 28).

Jesus answers, “You are mistaken because you do not know the Scriptures or the power of God” (verse 29). In the resurrection people will neither marry nor be given in marriage. They will be like the angels in heaven. And about the dead rising, have they not read what God said to them: ‘I am the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob’? “He is not the God of the dead, but of the living.” The crowds are astonished at his teaching.
passages.hearers:
Mark tells this scene too (Mark 12:18-27), and the note on Mark 12 explains it. The Sadducees were a small but powerful group linked with the high priest (Acts 5:17). The Jewish historian Josephus says they believed the soul dies with the body, and that they kept only what the written law commanded (Antiquities 18.16). Acts adds that they denied the resurrection, angels and spirits (Acts 23:8).

Their story is meant to make belief in the resurrection look silly. Many Jews of the time did believe God would raise the dead. One Jewish book, 2 Maccabees, tells of seven brothers who died under a cruel king rather than break God's law, trusting that God would raise them to new life (2 Maccabees 7). The Sadducees' seven brothers may be a mocking echo of that story.

Matthew tells it more briefly than Mark. He says God's words were spoken ‘to you’: the Scripture is addressing the Sadducees themselves. And he ends with the crowds astonished at Jesus' teaching.
passages.ot:
The law the Sadducees quote is Deuteronomy 25:5-6. If a man died with no son, his brother was to marry the widow, so that “his name will not be blotted out from Israel.” The book of Ruth shows a related custom.

Daniel had promised, “many who sleep in the dust of the earth will awake, some to everlasting life” (Daniel 12:2). But Jesus answers from the books of Moses, the part of Scripture the Sadducees held most firmly. At the burning bush, long after Abraham, Isaac and Jacob had died, God says, “I am the God of your father, the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob” (Exodus 3:6). God does not say ‘I was’. If he is still their God, they are not finished.
passages.hard:
Does this mean there will be no marriage in heaven, and that husbands and wives will not know each other? Christians read verse 30 in a few ways. Many take it plainly: marriage as we know it belongs to this age, when people die and need children to carry on. In the resurrection no one dies, so the reason for marriage as an institution is gone (compare Luke 20:36). Others stress what Jesus does not say. He does not say love is lost, or that people will not know one another, or that they will become angels. They will be ‘like’ the angels in this one way. Many believers hope that the love of this life will be fulfilled, not erased. The text does not settle every question, and it is wise not to claim more than it says.

For anyone grieving a husband or wife, this verse can feel cold. It is not meant to. Jesus' whole point is that God is the God of the living, and that the dead in him are not lost.

And if you have married again after a husband or wife died, this passage is not a judgment on you. Scripture says plainly that a widow is free to marry again (1 Corinthians 7:39). The Sadducees used a woman married seven times as a puzzle to mock the resurrection. Jesus does not treat her as a problem to be sorted out in heaven. Their puzzle falls apart because the life to come is not a rerun of this one.
passages.asks: The Sadducees used a puzzle to keep God small. Jesus said their problem was that they did not know the power of God. Ask whether you have made God only as big as what seems possible to you. And if you are grieving, hold on to the name God gave himself: the God of the living.

passages.t: The greatest commandment: love God, love your neighbour
passages.happening:
When the Pharisees hear that Jesus has silenced the Sadducees, they gather together. One of them, an expert in the law, tests him with a question: “Teacher, which commandment is the greatest in the Law?” (verse 36).

Jesus answers: ‘Love the Lord your God with all your heart and with all your soul and with all your mind.’ “This is the first and greatest commandment” (verse 38). And the second is like it: ‘Love your neighbor as yourself.’ Then he adds, “All the Law and the Prophets hang on these two commandments” (verse 40).
passages.hearers:
Mark tells this scene too (Mark 12:28-34), and the note on Mark 12 explains it. The first words Jesus quotes come from the Shema, named from the Hebrew word for ‘Hear’. It was, and still is, the heart of Jewish prayer, said each evening and each morning. The law told Israel to speak these words “when you lie down and when you get up” (Deuteronomy 6:7).

Asking for the heart of the law was a real question among Jewish teachers. The Talmud, written down centuries later, tells of the great teacher Hillel summing up the whole law for a Gentile: what is hateful to you, do not do to your neighbour (Shabbat 31a). A later teacher, Rabbi Akiva, is remembered for calling ‘love your neighbor as yourself’ a great principle of the law.

Matthew tells it differently from Mark. In Mark a scribe asks warmly, agrees with Jesus, and is told he is not far from the kingdom. In Matthew the questioner is testing him, and there is no reply. But Matthew alone keeps Jesus' last words: all the Law and the Prophets ‘hang’ on these two, like a door hanging on its hinges. Jesus said something similar in the Sermon on the Mount, of treating others as you would want to be treated: “this is the essence of the Law and the Prophets” (7:12).
passages.ot: Jesus joins two verses from different books. Deuteronomy 6:4-5: “Hear, O Israel: The LORD our God, the LORD is One. And you shall love the LORD your God with all your heart and with all your soul and with all your strength.” And Leviticus 19:18: “love your neighbor as yourself.” The verse in Leviticus begins, “Do not seek revenge or bear a grudge against any of your people.” Love of neighbour in the law was not a feeling but a way of treating people.
passages.asks: Jesus does not give a new commandment here. He gives the oldest ones, and says everything else hangs on them. Ask whether your faith has become busy with lesser things while love of God and love of neighbour run thin. Then ask who your neighbour is this week, and what loving them would cost.

passages.happening:
While the Pharisees are still gathered, Jesus asks them a question. “What do you think about the Christ? Whose son is He?” “David’s,” they answer. Jesus says, “How then does David in the Spirit call Him ‘Lord’?” (verse 43). For David says: ‘The Lord said to my Lord, “Sit at My right hand until I put Your enemies under Your feet.”’ “So if David calls Him ‘Lord,’ how can He be David’s son?” (verse 45).

No one can answer a word. From that day on no one dares to ask him any more questions.
passages.hearers:
Mark tells this scene too (Mark 12:35-37), and the note on Mark 12 explains it. Everyone agreed that the Messiah, the promised king, would come from David's family. In Matthew, Jesus puts the question to the Pharisees directly, and they give the answer everyone knew.

Matthew's readers have heard ‘Son of David’ all through the book. The book opens by calling Jesus “the son of David” (1:1). Blind men, a Canaanite mother, and the crowds at the gate have all called him by that title (9:27; 15:22; 21:9). Now Jesus asks what the title means.

A father would not normally call his own son ‘lord’. The son honoured the father. So if David calls this future king ‘my Lord’, the king must be more than David's son. Jesus is asking his hearers to think bigger.

This is the last of the questions. Matthew has told a run of them in the temple courts: about authority, about taxes, about the resurrection, about the greatest commandment. Now Jesus asks one of his own, and the questioning ends.
passages.ot: Psalm 110:1 reads: “The LORD said to my Lord: ‘Sit at My right hand until I make Your enemies a footstool for Your feet.’” God had promised David a son whose throne would last forever: “I will establish the throne of his kingdom forever” (2 Samuel 7:13).
passages.hard:
Does Jesus' argument depend on David writing the psalm, and is he denying that the Messiah is David's son? Readers answer in different ways. Many modern scholars think Psalm 110 was first written for a king of Judah by a court poet, not by David himself. Others, including many evangelical and Catholic scholars, hold to David as its author, as the psalm's heading says. A third view holds that Jesus argued from what his hearers already accepted, whoever first wrote the psalm, and that his point stands either way.

On the second question, Jesus does not deny that the Messiah is David's son. Matthew has called him that from the first verse of the book. Jesus asks how the Messiah can be both David's son and David's Lord. The early Christians answered with the resurrection. Paul says Jesus was “a descendant of David according to the flesh” and was “declared with power to be the Son of God by His resurrection from the dead” (Romans 1:3-4).
passages.asks: It is easy to fit Jesus into a title we already understand. Jesus pushes back: he is more than you think. Ask whether your picture of Jesus has grown smaller than he is, and what it would mean to call him ‘Lord’ and not only ‘teacher’ or ‘example’.
